cards.explanation: The answer is wise. Joab sends to Tekoa to bring back a wise woman (2 Samuel 14:2). I think he needed someone who could carry a story to a king without tripping over it. Grabbing the first person he saw wouldn't have cut it, friends.

The answer is False. The oil stays in the bottle. Joab says, “put on clothes for mourning and do not anoint yourself with oil.” (2 Samuel 14:2) He wants her to act like a woman who has mourned for the dead a long time. No glow, no shine, just the part.
The answer is Joab's words. The verse says it plainly: “And Joab put the words in her mouth.” (2 Samuel 14:3) So her sad story is a script, friends. She's basically reading cue cards to a king.
The answer is True. Her first words are “Help me, O king!” (2 Samuel 14:4) She falls facedown first, and then she cries out. Whatever else is going on, she opens like someone who needs help.

The answer is False. No one stepped in. In her story the two sons were fighting in the field “…with no one to separate them…” (2 Samuel 14:6) Then one struck the other and killed him. I think that detail makes the story hit harder.

The answer is that they plan to put him to death for his brother's life. The clan says, “Hand over the one who struck down his brother, that we may put him to death for the life of the brother whom he killed.” (2 Samuel 14:7) It's a life for a life, and the clan wants it done. The widow only has one son left.

The answer is name. She says they would “…extinguish my one remaining ember by not preserving my husband’s name or posterity on the earth.” (2 Samuel 14:7) Her husband is already dead, so her last son carries it all. I think that's why she calls him her one remaining ember.

The answer is False. She takes the blame herself. She says, “…may any blame be on me and on my father’s house, and may the king and his throne be guiltless.” (2 Samuel 14:9) That's a big offer to make to a king. Hold on to it, friends, because she's not done talking.

The answer is that not a hair of his head will fall. David vows by the LORD: “not a hair of your son’s head will fall to the ground.” (2 Samuel 14:11) A vow sworn by the LORD is serious business. And it's exactly what she asked for.

The answer is not bringing back his own banished son. She asks, “…does he not convict himself, since he has not brought back his own banished son?” (2 Samuel 14:13) She starts with a story about a family and ends by pointing at the king's own. That's quite the turn.

The answer is True. She says, “Yet God does not take away a life, but He devises ways that the banished one may not be cast out from Him.” (2 Samuel 14:14) She says it right after bringing up David's banished son (2 Samuel 14:13). I think she wants the king to hear it for himself.

The answer is inheritance. She says a man would “…cut off both me and my son from God’s inheritance.” (2 Samuel 14:16) It echoes the clan's plan to cut off the heir (2 Samuel 14:7). I think it's about more than land, friends. It's about having a place among God's people.

The answer is False. She owns up. David asks, “Is the hand of Joab behind all this?” (2 Samuel 14:19) And she says, “…Joab is the one who gave me orders; he told your maidservant exactly what to say.” No dodging. The truth comes out.

The answer is go and bring back Absalom. David tells Joab, “I hereby grant this request. Go, bring back the young man Absalom.” (2 Samuel 14:21) Joab wrote the script, and now he's the one getting the order. The plan worked.

The answer is Jerusalem. Joab got up, went to Geshur, and brought Absalom to Jerusalem (2 Samuel 14:23). Verse 28 says Absalom lived in Jerusalem two years (2 Samuel 14:28). So that's where the trip ends.

The answer is that he must not see the king's face. David says, “He may return to his house, but he must not see my face.” (2 Samuel 14:24) So Absalom is home, but he doesn't see his father. Close by, and still shut out.

The answer is that he refuses to come. Joab “…refused to come to him.” (2 Samuel 14:29) Absalom sent for him, and Joab just wouldn't show. Joab is the one who helped bring Absalom back, so you'd expect a visit, friends. Not this time.

The answer is False. Still no. Absalom sends a second time, and “…Joab still would not come.” (2 Samuel 14:29) That's two messages and nobody at the door. I think a person could get pretty annoyed by that.
The answer is set it on fire. Absalom tells his servants, “Go and set it on fire!” (2 Samuel 14:30) And they do. That's not a subtle way of saying, “please answer my message.”

The answer is Geshur. Absalom says, “Why have I come back from Geshur? It would be better for me if I were still there.” (2 Samuel 14:32) I think he means being home without seeing the king feels worse than being away. That's a sad thing to say.

The answer is True. Absalom says, “So now, let me see the king’s face, and if there is iniquity in me, let him kill me.” (2 Samuel 14:32) He asks to see the king's face, and he adds that if there is iniquity in him, the king should kill him. That's a bold thing to say.

The answer is that he kisses Absalom. After Absalom bows facedown, “Then the king kissed Absalom.” (2 Samuel 14:33) After two years of not seeing the king's face, that's a big moment, friends. I think it means a lot.
